The body mass of these newly emerged individuals is exceptionally low, with neonates weighing approximately 0.0048 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0048 grams], a value derived from the volume of the spherical, demersal eggs which measure about 2.1 millimeters in diameter. This minimal initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to support the early, non-feeding stage and stands in stark contrast to the more substantial size attained later in life.

The ultimate total length attained by adults is 11.5 centimeters [Li = 11.5 centimeters], a modest size that is typical for members of the genus. This final mass is achieved through a prolonged period of somatic investment that extends well beyond the point of puberty. The growth curve plateaus as the fish approach this asymptotic size, with the energy budget being increasingly directed toward reproductive functions rather than further increases in body length and mass. Field surveys in the Niger River basin have shown that individuals approaching this maximum length are comparatively rare, likely due to the combined pressures of natural senescence and predation.

Under laboratory conditions held at a constant 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 2.5 years [am = approximately 2.5 years], a duration that is typical for small-bodied tropical freshwater teleosts.
